Cardiology and hematology · published research

Blood flow (promotion of)

Some small human studies report short-term increases in local blood flow after light exposure, while other measurements show little change. A recent wound study found different thermal responses in diabetic foot and venous ulcers, using temperature as an indirect measure of local perfusion.

Evidence summary

What the evidence suggests

Responses vary by wavelength, tissue, and population. The clearest human findings concern short-term microcirculatory measurements, and a recent chronic-wound review reported very low overall certainty across its trials.

Summary of the Evidence

A randomized study in healthy adults found increased hand microcirculatory flow after 830-nm near-infrared exposure, while 633-nm red light did not increase median flow. A separate wound trial found higher measured microcirculation after an eight-week LED course, whereas some studies of normal tissue reported no immediate change (Gavish et al. 2020; Frangez et al. 2017; Heu et al. 2013; Calin et al. 2021).

A 2026 systematic review of six randomized trials in chronic lower-limb wounds reported that some LED protocols increased microcirculation and improved wound measures, particularly for diabetic foot ulcers. The review rated the overall certainty very low because of inconsistency and indirectness. It informs the wound findings but does not resolve flow responses in other populations or body sites (Miranda et al. 2026).

Human and clinical evidence

In a randomized study of 20 healthy adults, five minutes of 830-nm near-infrared exposure was followed by higher median measured hand microcirculatory flow at the immediate and follow-up assessments. The 633-nm red-light group did not show an increase in median flow. Some participants responded more strongly, and baseline hand temperature helped explain this variation (Gavish et al. 2020).

A randomized crossover study of ten healthy men found a brief increase in blood flow after a 3-W, 360-J class-IV laser exposure. Sham treatment and the 1-W and 6-W settings did not produce the same change. This was an acute physiological measurement, not a test of lasting benefit (Larkin et al. 2012).

In a double-blind randomized study of 79 people with chronic lower-limb wounds, within-group microcirculation measurements increased after the LED course in diabetic and non-diabetic participants, while no significant change was reported in the lower-fluence broadband-light reference groups. The study also reported improved wound-bed scores (Frangez et al. 2017).

A prospective study assessed 33 wounds in 20 people with diabetic foot or venous ulcers using thermal imaging before and after PBM. Wound-bed temperature increased in diabetic foot ulcers but showed no significant change in venous ulcers. This thermal response is associated with microvascular response in the study but is not a direct blood-flow estimate (Gavish et al. 2026).

Other small studies of healthy feet and normal-skin oxygenation found no immediate significant flow or oxygenation change. The findings therefore differ by site, protocol, and population (Heu et al. 2013; Calin et al. 2021).

Animal evidence

Rabbit and rat experiments have examined collateral circulation, local flow, and microcirculation during tissue repair. They report model-specific changes under different protocols (Ihsan et al. 2005; Núñez et al. 2004). A chick-embryo experiment tested a proposed infrared-related flow mechanism rather than a clinical treatment (Li and Pollack 2023).

In-vitro evidence

One human study paired skin microcirculation measurements with laboratory work on nitric-oxide-related signaling during carbon-dioxide laser exposure. These results explore a possible mechanism but do not establish a general treatment effect (Shen et al. 2019).

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Reported sources include visible red light around 633–660 nm and near-infrared light around 780–890 nm. The 20-person flow study used 830 nm for five minutes, the class-IV study compared several power settings, and the chronic-wound trial used LED treatment three times weekly for eight weeks. The 2026 ulcer study used 808-nm pulsed light and tracked temperature changes over 30 minutes. These distinct protocols do not establish one optimal setting for promoting blood flow (Gavish et al. 2020; Larkin et al. 2012; Frangez et al. 2017; Gavish et al. 2026).

Interpretation

Short-term local flow increases appear in selected human settings, including a healthy-volunteer study and a chronic-wound trial. Normal-tissue studies also report null findings, and wound responses differ by ulcer type. The 2026 wound-focused review rated the evidence very low. Current results support protocol-specific research but do not show that measured flow changes reliably persist or improve broader health outcomes.

Clinical effect sizes (estimate)

In 20 healthy adults, 830-nm near-infrared exposure was followed by a 27% increase in median hand microcirculatory flow immediately and 54% during 20-minute follow-up. The 633-nm red-light group did not show an increase in median flow. Ten participants met the temperature-based responder definition (Gavish et al. 2020).

In 79 people with chronic lower-limb wounds, within-group microcirculation increased in the treated diabetic and non-diabetic groups after the higher-fluence LED course (p = 0.040 and p = 0.033), while no significant change was reported in the lower-fluence broadband-light reference groups. The accessible summary does not provide a between-group effect magnitude (Frangez et al. 2017).

In 20 people with 33 wounds, wound-bed temperature rose by 2.10 ± 2.25 °C in diabetic foot ulcers (p < 0.001) and 0.68 ± 2.49 °C in venous ulcers (p = 0.385). This is an indirect thermal measure associated with microvascular response, not a direct flow estimate (Gavish et al. 2026).

A 10-person crossover study found a brief flow increase after a 3-W, 360-J class-IV exposure, but not after sham, 1-W, or 6-W settings. The report did not provide a comparable numerical treatment-effect estimate (Larkin et al. 2012).

Certainty of evidence (estimate)

Low-to-moderate for short-term flow changes in selected settings. A small randomized study and a chronic-wound trial found increased microcirculation under specific protocols, and a wound-focused review reports potential microcirculation benefits.

Low for consistent responses across people or durable clinical benefit. Some normal-tissue measurements were null, wound responses differed by ulcer type, and the systematic review rated the chronic-wound evidence very low (Heu et al. 2013; Calin et al. 2021; Miranda et al. 2026).

Rationale for the certainty assessment

Evidence for selected short-term flow changes comes from small, protocol-specific human studies, including a randomized healthy-volunteer study and a chronic-wound LED trial. Other normal-tissue measurements were null, and the 2026 wound-focused review rated overall certainty very low because of inconsistency and indirectness. The evidence supports limited confidence in responses under selected conditions and low confidence in consistent or durable benefit (Gavish et al. 2020; Frangez et al. 2017; Miranda et al. 2026).
